newsitem.title: USA: Almost 800 Kurdish refugees arrive in Guam - U.S.
newsitem.headline: Almost 800 Kurdish refugees arrive in Guam - U.S.

text.p: The first planes carrying Kurdish refugees who worked for the United States in northern Iraq arrived on the Pacific island of Guam on Tuesday, the State Department said.

"The first two planes carrying respectively 469 and 323 people -- a total of 792 -- have arrived at Anderson Air Force Base in Guam today. The first group was comprised of 264 adults, 187 children, 18 infants. The second group had 198 adults, 105 children and 20 infants," spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
He said a third group of 465 people left Diyarbakir, Turkey, on Tuesday morning and later a fourth plane with 462 passengers also departed for Guam.

"This operation is proceeding on schedule. We believe that the last Kurdish person will be out of Turkey on one of these planes by tomorrow for arrival Thursday Guam time at Anderson Air Force Base," Burns said.

The United States began the airlift from Turkey of about 2,080 former employees in northern Iraq on Monday. The aim is to give the refugees a new life in the United States far from Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

Most of the refugees worked as employees of U.S. aid programmes and the U.S.-led air operation patrolling a no-fly zone for Iraqi aircraft in northern Iraq. Some are reported to have been engaged in U.S. intelligence activities.

They had been holed up in small hotels and private homes waiting to escape since Iraqi troops entered the Western-protected Kurdish area to help the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) take the city of Arbil from a rival faction on Aug. 31.
That move, boosting Saddam's control of a region where he had been ineffective for the past five years, prompted U.S. cruise missile strikes on Iraq in early September.
Following U.S.-Turkish negotiations, the former U.S. employees and their household dependents crossed the mountainous border from Iraq into Turkey over the weekend.

The decision to move the Kurds to Guam enables them to be considered for what is called "parole" into the United States without the preliminary decisions on visas and refugee status that would be necessary if they were processed overseas.
